title: Montana Senate Standoff Tests Democrats' Red-State Independent Strategy
excerpt: With an August 10 ballot deadline looming, Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead has rejected calls to drop out in favor of independent Seth Bodnar, threatening to split the anti-Republican vote in a race where polls show a unified challenge could make the seat competitive.
body:
• Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead has refused to drop out of Montana's open Senate race, defying party leaders who want to consolidate behind independent Seth Bodnar
  • Polls show Republican Kurt Alme leads comfortably in a three-way race but is statistically tied with Bodnar head-to-head — the split anti-Republican vote is the GOP's biggest advantage
  • The August 10 ballot withdrawal deadline is approaching with no resolution, part of a broader Democratic experiment of backing independents in red states from Nebraska to Alaska

Montana's open U.S. Senate race has become a test case for one of the Democratic Party's most unconventional midterm strategies — backing independent candidates over their own nominees in deep-red states — and right now, the experiment is failing.

Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead, an Air Force lieutenant colonel who won the party's June 2 primary with 43.7% of the vote, has flatly refused calls from Democratic leaders to step aside in favor of Seth Bodnar, a former Green Beret and University of Montana president running as an independent.

"I am never dropping out. Ever. Ever. Ever."

— Alani Bankhead, Democratic Senate nominee

At a June 15 press conference, Bankhead went further: "If dropping out was the right move to pave the way for a better candidate, I would absolutely do it. But Seth Bodnar is absolutely the last person on the face of the Earth I would ever drop out of this race for."

A Strategy Born of Desperation

The standoff reflects a broader Democratic reckoning with the party's brand in conservative America. Across red states — Nebraska, Alaska, Idaho, South Dakota, and Montana — Democratic operatives are quietly sidelining their own nominees in favor of independent candidates they believe have a better shot against Republicans.

https://x.com/sahilkapur/status/2082908241248575909

In Nebraska, Democratic Senate nominee Cindy Burbank has signaled she plans to leave the race to consolidate support behind independent Dan Osborn, who came within seven points of winning a Senate seat in 2024. The Democratic National Committee and its allies have quietly backed the approach.

"The Democratic Party's brand is awful right now," Democratic strategist Josh Schwerin told the Associated Press. "The combination of the brand problem and the existential nature of the threat that our country is facing requires us to have a big tent."

But Montana presents the messiest version of this strategy. Bodnar, backed by former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester — who famously called the Democratic label a "poison" to his past campaigns — has raised $3.2 million and built a campaign staffed by Tester's former team. Bankhead has raised just $58,000.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Polling makes the mathematical reality stark. In a three-way race, Republican nominee Kurt Alme — the former U.S. Attorney handpicked by retiring Sen. Steve Daines in a last-minute filing maneuver — leads with 41-49% of likely voters, while Bankhead and Bodnar split the anti-Republican vote roughly evenly, each drawing 22-27%.

But head-to-head polls between Alme and Bodnar show a dead heat. A July GQR poll gave Bodnar a 50-44% lead over Alme in a two-way race, while Tavern Research found them tied at 50-50. Even Bankhead performs better against Alme one-on-one, trailing 52-44% in the most recent head-to-head.

"Regardless, if Bodnar and Democrats can't get on the same page, Republicans are going to win this seat anyway," said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics.

Every major forecaster rates the race as Likely or Solid Republican, with Inside Elections and the Cook Political Report both calling it Solid R.

The Daines Maneuver

The seat opened up through political theater that still rankles both parties. Daines, the two-term Republican incumbent, withdrew his candidacy at 4:55 p.m. on March 5 — five minutes before the filing deadline — and endorsed Alme, who had filed minutes earlier. President Trump immediately endorsed Alme on Truth Social.

The maneuver was designed to prevent a top-tier Democrat like Tester or former governors Brian Schweitzer or Steve Bullock from entering the race. It worked: with the deadline closed, no heavyweight Democrat could file.

What's Next

The August 10 deadline for candidates to withdraw from the ballot is now just days away. Democratic leaders continue to pressure Bankhead to step aside, but she has shown no signs of budging. Montana's Secretary of State has weighed in on procedural questions about what would happen if Bankhead withdrew, adding a layer of legal uncertainty to an already volatile situation.

For Democrats nationally, Montana has become a cautionary tale. The independent strategy requires something the party has struggled to deliver: discipline and coordination among candidates who often have their own reasons — personal, political, and principled — for staying in the fight.

The race is the first open Senate contest in Montana since 1976, and with a 53-47 Republican Senate majority, every seat matters in Democrats' uphill battle to flip the chamber.
nri_angle: The Montana race is part of a broader reshaping of U.S. political strategy that could influence Senate control and policy affecting Indian Americans.
